Ḥad Gadya (Ein Zicklein), a German translation with commentary by Paul Christian Kirchner in his Jüdisches Ceremoniel (Nuremberg, 1717)

tei:div.tei:head: Ḥad Gadya (Ein Zicklein), a German translation with commentary by Paul Christian Kirchner in his Jüdisches Ceremoniel (Nuremberg, 1717)

tei:l.tei:note: Here are the ten Ḳabbalistic verses which the Jews recite with great devotion in Aramaic as well as in German on the first two paschal nights to mark the beginning of the ceremonies after the meal. Each verse must be spoken in Aramaic, and afterwards in Hebrew and German.

tei:lg.tei:l: One li’l kid, one li’l kid,
which my father bought
for two pennies,
a li’l kid.
Then the li’l cat came
and ate the li’l kid
that my li’l father had bought
for two li’l pennies,
one li’l kid.
Then the li’l dog came
and bit the li’l cat,
which had eaten the li’l kid
that my li’l father bought
for two li’l pennies,
one li’l kid.
Then the li’l stick came
and struck the li’l dog,
which had bitten the li’l cat,
which had eaten the li’l kid,
which had been bought
for two li’l pennies,
one li’l kid.
Then the fire came,
and burned the li’l stick;
with which the li’l dog was beaten,
because it had bit the li’l cat,
for eating the li’l kid,
which was bought by my li’l father
for two li’l pennies,
one li’l kid.
Then came the li’l water,
and extinguished the li’l fire,
which had burned the li’l stick,
that had beaten the li’l dog,
which had bitten the li’l cat,
that had eaten the li’l kid,
which my litte father had bought
for two li’l pennies,
one li’l kid.
Then came a li’l ox,
drank the li’l water,
that had extinguished the li’l fire,
that had burned the li’l stick,
with which had been beaten the li’l dog,
which had bitten the li’l cat,
because it had eaten the li’l kid,
which my li’l father had bought
for two li’l pennies,
one li’l kid.
Then came the slaughterer,
and slaughtered the li’l ox,
that had drank up the li’l water,
that had extinguished the li’l fire,
that had burned the li’l stick,
with which had been beaten the li’l dog,
because it had bitten the li’l cat,
because it had eaten the li’l kid,
which my li’l father had bought
for two li’l pennies,
one li’l kid.
Then came the Malakh ha-Mavet
(or the angel who is appointed to collect the souls of men
when their time comes for them to die),
and slaughtered the slaughterer,
who had slaugtered the li’l ox,
which had drank up the li’l water,
that had made extinguished the li’l fire,
for it had burned the li’l stick,
with which had been beaten the li’l dog,
because it had bitten the li’l cat,
which had eaten the li’l kid,
which my li’l father had bought
for two li’l pennies,
one li’l kid.
Then came God,
and slaughtered the angel
who is appointed to collect the souls of men,
who had slaughtered the slaughterer,
who had slaugtered the li’l ox,
which had drank the li’l water,
that extinguished the li’l fire,
which made burn the li’l stick,
with which had been beaten the li’l dog,
that had had bitten the li’l cat,
which had eaten the li’l kid,
which my li’l father had bought
for two li’l pennies,
one li’l kid.
A brief interpretation which many rabbis themselves hold to the ten prior-written verses, and thus indicate:
The kid represents the paschal lamb, the staff or stick represents the scepter, and the water represents the Holy Spirit who hovers over the water, taken from Genesis 1:2.

The ox signifies an ox that has eaten up a thousand mountains every day, which is called Shor haBor, for they state that all the pious and righteous will be fed of it when the Messiah comes. And through the li’l cat they understand that the quarreling and bickering hearts will be disturbed. The barking dog will awaken all hearts together so that they become awoken, and will be terrified at the judgment. They understand fire to mean that God is a fire, and consumes that of others; they got it from the Talmudic אֵשׁ אוֹכֶלֶת אֵשׁ which means “Fire consuming fire.” They also establish from these three Talmudic words that there are two hells, namely the first and highest one, which is called Hinnom, that is purgatory, and the other they call the lowest hell שְׁאוֹל תַּחְתִּיָּה. And they maintain that no matter how someone may have lived, even as a prophet, they must still end up in the highest hell. I, along with all Protestant Christians, consider this a fable, as it is nothing else, but the Jews consider it a great mystery and celebrate it with great devotion.

tei:note.tei:p: Kirchner, who was an apostate who had converted to Christianity.
